title: Fewest Edits to a Strong Password
statement:
A sign-up form accepts a password only if it is strong:

  • it has between 6 and 20 characters, inclusive;
  • it contains at least one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter and one digit;
  • it never has the same character three times in a row ("xx7xx" is fine, "x777" is not).

One edit inserts a character, deletes a character, or replaces a character with another. Return the fewest edits that turn password into a strong password. A password that is already strong needs 0.

examples.why: It already has all three kinds of character, but it is 3 characters short. Three inserts are needed and enough.
Replacing the third z with an uppercase letter and the sixth with a digit fixes the run and both missing kinds at once.
22 characters, nothing else wrong. Two deletions bring it to 20.

constraints: password contains only letters, digits, '.' and '!'
hints: Handle the three length regimes separately: too short, fine, too long. In each one, which edit can fix two problems at once?

When the length is fine, a replacement inside a run fixes the run and can supply a missing character kind. A run of length L needs L / 3 (rounded down) replacements. When the password is too short, inserts play that role.

When it is too long, you must delete n − 20 characters anyway. Spend them inside runs where they save replacements: first runs with L % 3 = 0 (1 deletion saves a replacement), then L % 3 = 1 (2 deletions), then 3 deletions per replacement.

explain.intuition:
Three problems, three edit types, and the art is in letting one edit fix two problems. A run of length L can be broken with ⌊L / 3⌋ replacements (change every third character), and each of those replacements can also be the missing uppercase letter or digit. So when the length is already fine, the answer is max(missing kinds, replacements for runs).

If the password is too short (under 6), inserts fix everything: each insert adds length, can break a run, and can add a missing kind; with at most 5 characters there is never a long enough run to need more. Answer: max(missing, 6 − n). If it is too long, n − 20 deletions are unavoidable, so make them count. A deletion inside a run with L % 3 = 0 lowers ⌊L / 3⌋ immediately. For L % 3 = 1 it takes two deletions, and after that every run needs three deletions per saved replacement. Spend deletions in that order, then pay max(missing, remaining replacements).
steps: Count the missing kinds (lowercase, uppercase, digit): missing is 0 to 3.
Scan runs of equal characters of length ≥ 3. Add ⌊L / 3⌋ to replace, and count runs with L % 3 = 0 (one) and L % 3 = 1 (two).
Let del = n − 20. Subtract min(del, one) from replace; then min(max(del − one, 0), 2 · two) / 2; then max(del − one − 2 · two, 0) / 3 (integer division throughout).
pitfalls: Deleting characters from runs in any order. Deleting from a run of length 3k + 2 first wastes deletions that could have saved a replacement elsewhere.
Breaking a long run with deletions alone when the password is short or just right. Replacements are cheaper: one replacement breaks three characters' worth of run.
Adding the missing kinds on top of the run replacements. A replacement can do both jobs, so take the max, not the sum.

solutions.title: Dynamic programming over edits
solutions.idea: Walk the password and, at each position, try to keep, delete or replace the character, or insert a new one. Track the output length, the last original character and its run length, and which kinds are present. New characters are chosen to differ from their neighbours, so they never extend a run.

solutions.title: Greedy case analysis
solutions.idea: Too short: inserts fix everything. Right length: replacements fix runs and missing kinds together. Too long: spend the forced deletions where they save the most replacements, by run length mod 3.

followups: Return one strong password that uses the minimum number of edits, not just the count.
The minimum length becomes 8 and runs of 4 are forbidden instead of 3. Which numbers in the greedy change?
